summary: Morphine is the prototypical mu-opioid agonist used for acute and chronic pain severe enough to require an opioid when alternatives are inadequate. It provides potent analgesia but carries a boxed warning for addiction, abuse, misuse, life-threatening respiratory depression, neonatal opioid withdrawal, and fatal interaction with benzodiazepines/CNS depressants. It is a Schedule II controlled substance and is habit forming. Active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment.
indications: Management of acute pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic when alternatives are inadequate (patients >=50 kg for the tablet)
Management of chronic pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic when alternative treatments are inadequate (adults)

moa: Morphine is an agonist principally at mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system and elsewhere. Receptor activation inhibits ascending pain pathways and alters the perception and emotional response to pain, producing analgesia along with sedation, euphoria, respiratory depression, and reduced gastrointestinal motility. Active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide contributes to analgesia and toxicity.

absolute: Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or without resuscitative equipment
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction including paralytic ileus
relative: Head injury or raised intracranial pressure

preg: Use only if clearly needed. Prolonged use during pregnancy can cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if unrecognised. Use near delivery may cause neonatal respiratory depression. Discuss risks individually.
lact: Morphine is excreted in breast milk. Occasional low maternal doses may be compatible, but repeated or higher dosing risks infant sedation and respiratory depression - monitor the infant closely and prefer the lowest effective dose.
renal: Use with caution and reduce dose or extend the dosing interval, because the active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates in renal impairment and can cause prolonged sedation and respiratory depression.
hepatic: Clearance is reduced in hepatic impairment; reduce the dose and titrate cautiously to avoid accumulation and excessive sedation.

major: Benzodiazepines and other CNS depressants (profound sedation, respiratory depression, death)
Alcohol (including ER formulations - dose dumping risk)
Other opioids / mixed agonist-antagonists (withdrawal or additive effects)

pearls: Schedule II controlled substance - HABIT FORMING with boxed warning for addiction, abuse, misuse, and fatal respiratory depression
Active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates in renal impairment - reduce dose/extend interval
Boxed warning: benzodiazepines/CNS depressants plus morphine can cause fatal respiratory depression

missed: For regularly scheduled (e.g. extended-release) dosing, take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is close to the next dose, then skip it - never double up. For as-needed dosing, take only when in pain. If you miss several doses or are unsure, contact your prescriber.
overdose: Overdose causes the classic triad of pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and decreased consciousness, progressing to apnoea, hypotension, and death. It is a medical emergency: support the airway and ventilation and give naloxone, repeating as needed since morphine's effects can outlast a single naloxone dose. Continuous monitoring is required.
